Red flag present (abdominal pain, neurological symptoms or peritonism)?
Urgent surgical review for bowel infarction or perforation
Skin biopsy for wedge-shaped ischaemic necrosis; antiphospholipid and ANA testing
Does biopsy show thrombosed vessel necrosis with mimics excluded?
Consider antiphospholipid syndrome, lupus vasculopathy or cholesterol embolisation
Aspirin and dipyridamole for the cutaneous-only variant
Eculizumab and treprostinil for systemic disease
Surveillance with endoscopy or imaging and brain MRI for systemic spread
Skin care and analgesia for atrophic lesions
Cutaneous-only form may persist for years; systemic form carries a poor prognosis

cells.text: Wedge-shaped ischaemic dermal necrosis over a thrombosed vessel

rows.parameter: Antiphospholipid antibody and lupus anticoagulant testing

cells.text: Excludes antiphospholipid syndrome as a mimic
Excludes lupus and other connective-tissue mimics
Confused with Degos disease; separated by antiphospholipid testing
Lupus vasculopathy; separated by ANA and connective-tissue serology
Degos is a vasculopathy, not a true inflammatory vasculitis
Early non-specific papules, which are easily dismissed
First-line for the benign cutaneous-only variant to limit thrombo-occlusion
For systemic disease, targeting C5b-9-mediated endothelial injury
Prostacyclin analogue to improve microvascular perfusion
Endoscopy or imaging and brain MRI to detect bowel and CNS involvement early
Surgery for bowel infarction or perforation; neurological care for cerebral ischaemia
Dermatology, gastroenterology, neurology and rheumatology; specialist centre if systemic

nodes.text: Postmenopausal woman, older man, fracture or glucocorticoid use
Low-trauma hip or vertebral fracture?
DXA of spine and hip, with FRAX
T-score -2.5 or lower, or FRAX hip 3% or MOF 20% or more?
Lifestyle, calcium and vitamin D; repeat DXA later
Labs for secondary causes and treat any found
Very high risk (T under -3.0 or multiple vertebral fractures)?
Anabolic agent: teriparatide, abaloparatide or romosozumab
Follow with an antiresorptive to consolidate gains
Oral bisphosphonate first line; zoledronic acid or denosumab if unsuitable
Reassess at 3 to 5 years for drug holiday; never stop denosumab abruptly

valueTables.title: Diagnosing osteoporosis and setting the treatment threshold

cells.text: Low bone density; a risk factor for osteoporosis
-2.5 or lower at lumbar spine, femoral neck or total hip
Low-trauma hip, vertebral, humerus or distal radius fracture
Low for age; look for secondary causes
Estrogen-deficient women at risk; x-ray osteopenia or vertebral fracture; glucocorticoid 7.5 mg/day prednisone equivalent or more, or over 3 months; primary hyperparathyroidism; monitoring therapy
Repeat BMD at intervals over 23 months unless justified sooner
Calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, 25(OH)D, ALP, PTH, creatinine, 24 h urine calcium, testosterone in men
Add TSH, cortisol, SPEP and free light chains, tTG IgA when suspected

valueTables.footnote: Treatment thresholds by FRAX are the US values; other countries set their own intervention thresholds.

valueTables.title: Conditions that mimic or cause low bone mass

cells.text: Bone pain, proximal weakness, low mineral to matrix ratio
Bone pain, punched-out lesions, anemia, can mimic generalized osteoporosis
SPEP, serum free light chains, urine protein electrophoresis
Most common drug cause of osteoporosis
24 h urinary free cortisol or dexamethasone suppression test
Cyclosporine, cytotoxics, anticonvulsants, alcohol excess, aromatase inhibitors, excess thyroxine, aluminum, GnRH agonists, heparin, lithium
Bone spurs falsely raise spine BMD
Use hip sites; review vertebral imaging
Calcium at least 1000 mg/day, 1200 mg/day for postmenopausal women and older men; vitamin D 600 to 800 IU/day, aim 25(OH)D 30 ng/mL or more

rows.parameter: Exercise, fall prevention, stop smoking, limit alcohol

cells.text: Empty stomach, full glass of water, upright 30 min or more; needs CrCl over 35 mL/min; usual course 5 years
{{hy:Never stop without a follow-on antiresorptive}}; rebound vertebral fractures; no drug holiday
Very high risk: T-score under -3.0, multiple vertebral fractures, antiresorptive failure
Daily subcutaneous, about 2 years, then an antiresorptive
Monthly for 1 year; avoid within 12 months of MI or stroke; follow with antiresorptive
Postmenopausal women with mainly vertebral risk
Cuts vertebral but not hip fractures; raises thromboembolism risk
After 3 years IV or 5 years oral bisphosphonate in lower-risk patients
Consider 5 to 10 years if fractures or ongoing high risk
